The total storage capacity required for the resulting BAM, annotated VCF, and CNV files is approximately 1.378 TB (reported as about 1.4 TB).
This breakdown includes 530 GB for mapping/merging/deduplication, 386 GB for quality score recalibration, and 4 GB for variant calling and annotation .

If any component in the chain (e.g., a software version or a parameter in a previous step) changes, the hash for that job and all subsequent downstream jobs will change, preventing the use of stale or incorrect cached results .
This allows a user to benefit from results generated by a different workflow, a different project, or even a different user, provided the job definition and inputs are identical .

This approach is particularly effective for shared datasets, such as reference genomes or common post-processing steps, which frequently reoccur across different scientific analyses within an institution .

This approach allows the workflow engine to bundle multiple connected jobs from the Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) into a single "group job" submitted as one unit to the middleware (such as SLURM, Kubernetes, or AWS Batch) .
This significantly reduces the overhead caused by queuing delays, environment initialization, and remote storage access for short-running jobs .
Methodologically, it shifts from BAM to CRAM file formats (reducing storage by 66%) and optimizes task scattering (reducing intermediate storage by 5x) [03_nfcore_framework.pdf:10, 11].

Enhanced intra-sample parallelization reduces runtime by nearly 75% (from ~46 hours to ~12 hours for a standard WGS sample), resulting in a total compute cost reduction of 69–70% [03_nfcore_framework.pdf:0, 11].

fastp achieves high performance and low I/O overhead through an all-in-one design that performs quality control, trimming, and filtering in a single scan of the data, eliminating redundant I/O cycles [04_fastp.pdf:0, p. 884].

Additionally, fastp integrates specialized tasks like UMI preprocessing and output sharding into its main processing loop and uses efficient sampling techniques for overrepresented sequence analysis to maintain speed without sacrificing accuracy [04_fastp.pdf:0, p. 886, 887].
In a speed evaluation on a 9,316 M base dataset, the processing time for fastp (PE) was 13.3 minutes, while the processing time for Trimmomatic (PE) was 60.9 minutes .
Overlap Detection: The algorithm seeks the overlapping region between Read 1 and Read 2.

Sensitivity: A significant advantage of this overlap-based method is that it can detect and trim even very short adapter fragments (as short as 1 or 2 bp) in the read tail, which traditional sequence-matching tools often miss .

For large-scale projects, MultiQC ensures usability by automatically adapting its rendering method—switching from interactive JavaScript plots to static images as sample numbers increase to maintain performance .
Additionally, an interactive toolbox allows researchers to highlight, hide, or filter samples, making it easier to spot patterns in irregular data groups .

This facilitates the detection of splice junctions (by mapping different parts of a read to donor/acceptor sites), mismatches and indels (by using MMPs as anchors for extension and stitching), and chimeric/fusion transcripts (by identifying MMPs that map to distal genomic loci) [source_file:06_star_aligner.pdf:0, 4].
Additionally, it identifies non-genomic features like poly-A tails, library adapters, and poor-quality tails when an MMP cannot be extended into a valid genomic alignment .
This mapping speed outperforms the second-fastest aligner, TopHat2 (10.1 million read pairs/hour), by a factor of more than 50 [source_file:06_star_aligner.pdf, page:0].
Other compared aligners were even slower, including RUM (7.6 million), MapSplice (3.1 million), and GSNAP (2.8 million) [source_file:06_star_aligner.pdf, page:0].

These corrections lead to markedly higher sensitivity (53% to 450% higher than kallisto at the same FDR) and a significant reduction in false positives (producing fewer than half as many false DE calls as other methods when testing technical confounds) [source_file:07_salmon.pdf:0, pages 2, 21].

Additionally, Salmon's bias-aware estimates eliminate false "isoform switching" events that are often incorrectly detected by other quantifiers due to uncorrected technical variation [source_file:07_salmon.pdf:0, page 12].

Salmon achieves its performance through a combination of quasi-mapping (a lightweight mapping procedure that tracks position and orientation), a dual-phase inference strategy (online stochastic estimation followed by offline refinement), and the use of rich equivalence classes that factorize the likelihood function while preserving bias information [source_file:07_salmon.pdf:3, 9, 13].

Key optimizations include the use of concurrent cuckoo hash maps for thread-safe data management and mini-batch "laissez-faire" updates to ensure high-speed parallel processing across multiple CPU cores [source_file:07_salmon.pdf:11, 12].

In the reproducibility analysis using the Bottomly et al. dataset split into two independent halves, the overlap of the top 100 genes (ranked by the strongest up- or down-regulation) improved from 21 out of 100 genes when using standard MLE estimates to 81 out of 100 genes when using shrunken MAP estimates .

Compared to the ordinary log transformation, which allows low-count genes to exhibit high variance and exaggerated fold changes due to noise, the rlog transformation shrinks these low-count values toward a baseline while maintaining standard log-scale behavior for high-count genes.

SeqKit achieves stable memory usage and high efficiency through several key algorithmic and structural optimizations, specifically designed to handle large-scale genomic datasets without loading entire files into RAM.

In tests with files significantly larger than the human genome, SeqKit's memory usage remained constant at approximately 750–780 Mb because it processes records iteratively [09_seqkit.pdf:0 (page 8)].
This contrasts with tools like `seqmagick`, which read entire files into memory and can exhaust system resources on large datasets [09_seqkit.pdf:0 (page 7)].
Hardware Efficiency: While SeqKit is designed to be lightweight, it is optimized for multi-core environments.
It uses multiple Goroutines to parallelize CPU-intensive tasks (such as sequence validation and reverse complement computation) and defaults to using two threads on multi-core computers .
Accessibility: Users can download the executable binary files directly from its repository (e.g., GitHub) and run them from the command line .

Cutadapt balances trade-offs by using a hybrid implementation: it is primarily written in Python to ensure ease of use, maintenance, and the addition of user-requested features, while the performance-heavy alignment algorithm is written in C as a Python extension for speed .
However, this implementation creates a bottleneck where I/O operations (reading/parsing) often consume more than half of the processing time .
It also distinguishes itself from many peers by supporting gapped alignments to handle insertions and deletions (common in 454 data) and being able to identify partial adapter matches.

Researchers used a hierarchical multi-gene analysis targeting the *p72 (B646L), p54 (E183L), CD2v (EP402R), and B602L (CVR) genes to establish genetic identity [source_file:11_asf_burkina_faso.pdf:4, 8].
Analysis of the p72 gene classified the strains as Genotype I, while the p54 gene further refined this to genotype Ia [source_file:11_asf_burkina_faso.pdf:4, 10].

Finally, the Central Variable Region (CVR) of the B602L gene was analyzed for tetrameric repeat sequences (TRS), identifying four distinct variants and establishing epidemiological links between different outbreak locations [source_file:11_asf_burkina_faso.pdf:3, 6, 9].
These targets were analyzed using phylogenetic methods such as Neighbor-Joining, Minimum Evolution, and Maximum Likelihood trees in MEGA 7* [source_file:11_asf_burkina_faso.pdf:7, 10].

Analysis of the Central Variable Region (CVR) identified four tetrameric repeat sequence (TRS) variants (12, 23, 24, and 32 TRS), which were distinct from ten variants previously found in the country [11_asf_burkina_faso.pdf:7, 9].
According to the study, the clinical presentations and mortality detection thresholds for HPAI differ significantly between chicken (Galliformes) and duck (Anseriformes) populations as follows:
Physical Symptoms: Chickens more frequently exhibit mucosal membrane and skin signs, such as cyanosis and hemorrhagic conjunctiva [12_hpai_netherlands.pdf:2, 8].
The distribution of HPAI outbreaks in meat-type poultry increased from 6.3% in the 2014–2018 period to 39.5% in the 2020–2022 period [12_hpai_netherlands.pdf:0 (Table 4)].

This represents a specific percentage increase of 527.0% (or a 33.2 percentage point increase) in the distribution of infected meat-type poultry farms between the two periods [12_hpai_netherlands.pdf:0, 6].

The Mortality Ratio (MR) is defined as the ratio of a flock's daily mortality to its average daily mortality from the preceding week, used as an early warning signal for HPAI [source_file:12_hpai_netherlands.pdf:0, 6].

To calculate it, researchers first added 0.1 to all daily mortality percentages (to avoid calculation issues with zero values) and then divided the mortality percentage of the day before notification by the average mortality percentage of the previous seven days [source_file:12_hpai_netherlands.pdf:0, 10].
Other symptoms included fever, enlarged lymph nodes, and nasal/ocular discharges .
The Simple Intradermal Tuberculin Test (SITT) at 4 mm yielded a prevalence of 1.8%, indicating that CIDT at the standard threshold may under-detect cases by filtering out cross-reactions .

4 mm threshold: 1.8% (3/160 cattle; 95% CI: 0%–3.6%) .
However, the most detailed results section specifies 11 CIDT positives (3mm), 3 SITT positives (4mm), and 1 CIDT positive (4mm) .

The clinical presentations and relative frequency of H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b infections differ significantly between mammals and humans, characterized by widespread mass mortality in the former and rare, often milder, sporadic cases in the latter.
Mammals: Infections have reached unprecedented levels globally, affecting a broad range of species including skunks, foxes, bears, mink, seals, sea lions, and domestic cattle [19:0].
In the United States, clade 2.3.4.4b has also caused a widespread multi-state outbreak in dairy cattle.
Humans: Human cases remain extremely rare and sporadic despite the massive scale of avian and mammalian outbreaks [19:0].
As of mid-2024, only a small number of human infections (dozens globally) have been linked to clade 2.3.4.4b, a stark contrast to the millions of animals affected [19:0].
Manifestations include ataxia, tremors, and seizures [19:0].

However, in domestic livestock such as dairy cattle, the presentation is typically non-lethal, characterized by reduced appetite, lethargy, and changes in milk (thickened, discolored, or decreased production).
Ocular/Respiratory: Some mammals, particularly cats on infected dairy farms, have shown severe systemic illness, including pneumonia and blindness, often leading to death.

Ocular Symptoms (Conjunctivitis): In the most recent outbreaks associated with clade 2.3.4.4b (specifically the 2024 U.S. dairy cattle outbreak), conjunctivitis (eye redness and discomfort) has emerged as a predominant clinical sign in humans.
Mild Respiratory Disease: Many 2.3.4.4b cases in humans have been reported as mild respiratory infections, including symptoms like sore throat and cough.

Contrast with Historical H5N1: While historical H5N1 infections (pre-2020) were characterized by severe pneumonia and a mortality rate of approximately 50%, clade 2.3.4.4b human cases have generally (though not exclusively) trended toward milder presentations so far [19:0].
While most infected animals survive, the virus causes significant economic damage through milk loss, hide damage, and infertility .

Granular Resource Tracking: The framework uses detailed "trace" configurations to monitor CPU, memory, and disk usage per task, allowing for the fine-tuning of resource requests to avoid over-provisioning [03_nfcore_framework:0].

This algorithm optimizes execution based on a lexicographical priority: first, high-priority jobs; second, maximum parallelization (core usage); and third, the minimization of temporary file lifetime [02_snakemake:0].
This ensures that temporary files are deleted as soon as their consuming jobs are finished, which inherently optimizes disk space during runtime [02_snakemake:0].

Interaction with Middleware: While Snakemake can govern resources globally, it also passes specific resource requirements (threads, memory, disk usage) to cluster or cloud middleware like SLURM, Kubernetes, or AWS Batch, allowing these systems to choose the best-fitting machines [02_snakemake:0].

Readability: The system is designed to be highly readable, using a text-based format that builds on the Unix 'make' utility, making the logic of the data analysis transparent and adaptable for other researchers [02_snakemake:0].

The 'all-in-one' approach of fastp complements MultiQC by consolidating several preprocessing steps (trimming, filtering, and QC) into a single execution that produces a highly structured JSON report .

While fastp provides detailed pre- and post-filtering comparisons for individual samples to evaluate the effectiveness of data cleaning, MultiQC parses these JSON outputs to aggregate the metrics into a single, interactive global report .

This synergy allows bioinformaticians to use fastp for efficient data processing and then use MultiQC to quickly identify batch effects, outliers, and global trends across large datasets that would be difficult to spot in per-sample reports .

These include: 1) The use of Domain-Specific Languages (DSLs)—Nextflow for Sarek/nf-core and a Python-based DSL for Snakemake—to improve code readability and separate logic from execution . 2) Containerization via Docker and Singularity/Apptainer to encapsulate software environments . 3) Automated package management through Conda/Bioconda for dependency resolution . 4) Abstracted execution environments, providing native support for local HPC schedulers (Slurm, LSF, SGE) and cloud platforms (AWS, Google Cloud, Kubernetes) . 5) Modularization, such as Nextflow DSL2 modules, to promote code reuse and maintenance . 6) Resumability, allowing pipelines to restart from the point of failure . 7) Strict versioning and archival using GitHub and Zenodo to maintain historical records of pipeline states .

FastQ Sharding: `fastp` is used to split raw sequencing data into smaller chunks, allowing the mapping and deduplication steps to run in parallel across many nodes, which drastically reduces wall-clock time [03_nfcore_framework.pdf:0, 4].
The nf-core framework leverages the dataflow programming model of Nextflow, which is inherently decentralized and asynchronous.
Processes are executed as soon as their input "channels" receive a signal, allowing for a highly fluid execution where different parts of the pipeline can progress independently .

For instance, sarek 3.1.1 utilizes a dedicated process for splitting FastQ files and sharding them into interval groups (the default is 21 groups for variant calling) to maximize parallel job submission .
Snakemake employs a centralized scheduling approach based on dependency resolution and mathematical optimization.
It evaluates the entire Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of jobs and optimizes for four criteria in lexicographical order:
Parallelization: While earlier versions were single-threaded, `Cutadapt` supports multi-core processing by using multiple processes to handle blocks of reads .
Because it is built on a high-level language, `Cutadapt` is generally noted as being 3–5 times slower than `fastp` .
It also typically focuses on a narrower set of tasks (trimming) compared to the "all-in-one" approach of `fastp`, which means it often requires additional I/O passes when paired with other tools .

STAR addresses the challenge of spliced alignment and mapping accuracy by using a seed-and-stitch algorithm that identifies splice junctions and handles short overhangs that often lead to misalignments .

Together, they ensure that the count data fed into DESeq2 is free from common technical artifacts that would otherwise increase false positive rates or destabilize the shrinkage estimators used by DESeq2 for differential expression analysis .

Downstream, Cutadapt ensures mapping accuracy and prevents spurious alignment scores, while Salmon improves the reliability of differential expression analysis and reduces false discoveries of isoform switching .

** The integration of fastp and Cutadapt with MultiQC occurs through MultiQC's use of dedicated submodules that parse the per-sample logs and JSON outputs generated by these preprocessing tools [05_multiqc:0, 04_fastp:0].

This integration supports MultiQC's goals of identifying global trends, detecting batch effects, and highlighting outliers by aggregating disparate QC metrics—such as fastp’s pre- and post-filtering statistics—into a single, interactive, and comparative visualization report [05_multiqc:0, 04_fastp:0].

STAR utilizes a sequential search for Maximal Mappable Prefixes (MMP) implemented via uncompressed suffix arrays to achieve high-speed spliced alignment, trading high memory usage for logarithmic search times .
In contrast, SeqKit focuses on high-performance parsing and multithreading (Goroutines) to manipulate FASTA/Q files efficiently.
SeqKit's memory management is tied to the length of the longest sequence rather than total file size, allowing it to process large datasets through streaming and piping [09_seqkit.pdf:0,6,8].

Based on the provided documents, the diagnostic methodologies and biological markers used to determine the prevalence of bovine tuberculosis (bTB) and Peste des petits ruminants (PPR) in Cameroon and Ethiopia are contrasted by their reliance on field-based hypersensitivity tests versus laboratory-based serological assays.
Studies in Cameroon and Ethiopia utilize similar diagnostic standards for bTB, focusing on cellular immunity.

Methodological Optimization: In Cameroon, researchers found that a 3 mm threshold for CIDT increased sensitivity for detecting reactors compared to the 4 mm threshold recommended by the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) [source_file: 14_bovine_tb_cameroon.pdf, Page 0].

Delayed-Type Hypersensitivity (DTH): The biological marker is the localized inflammatory response (skin swelling) triggered by the injection of bovine and avian Purified Protein Derivatives (PPD) [source_file: 14_bovine_tb_cameroon.pdf, Page 0].
Ethiopia: Referenced studies indicate variable prevalence in dairy cattle across central and eastern Ethiopia, particularly in emerging "dairy belts" [source_file: 14_bovine_tb_cameroon.pdf, Page 0].
Molecular Detection: Studies also employ RT-PCR and other molecular techniques for the isolation and detection of the PPR virus (PPRV) [source_file: 16_ppr_ethiopia.pdf, Page 0].

PPRV Antibodies: The marker is the presence of specific antibodies, often targeting the viral nucleoprotein, indicating either natural infection or vaccination [source_file: 16_ppr_ethiopia.pdf, Page 0].
Ethiopia: In the Borena Zone, seroprevalence was 32.1% in non-vaccinated small ruminants and 68.8% in vaccinated animals [source_file: 16_ppr_ethiopia.pdf, Page 0].
Herd immunity levels were noted to be below the FAO-WOAH recommended 80% threshold for eradication [source_file: 16_ppr_ethiopia.pdf, Page 0].

The challenges of disease control in the Serengeti rabies campaigns—primarily the difficulty of achieving and maintaining a 70% coverage threshold in mobile populations—are exacerbated in LSD control by the lower efficacy of heterologous vaccines.
While homologous LSD vaccines are 100% effective, the widely used goat pox vaccines provide only 60–70% protection .

This lower efficacy requires even higher vaccination coverage to achieve herd immunity, a goal hindered by the same logistical barriers seen in the Serengeti: massive population sizes (e.g., 200 million cattle in India), animal movement, and spatial gaps** in vaccination efforts like ring vaccination .

The comparison between HPAI Clade 2.3.4.4 outbreaks in the Netherlands (2014–2022) and Canada (2022) reveals a shift from a primarily poultry-focused agricultural crisis to a multi-taxa ecological crisis with significant mammalian involvement.
Gallinaceous Poultry (Chickens/Turkeys): Predominantly characterized by high mortality rates (MR > 3%), which served as the primary trigger for clinical notifications .
Ecological Breadth: The Netherlands experienced HPAI as a persistent agricultural threat that gradually expanded into wild bird populations.

Seasonality: The Dutch outbreaks became "long-lasting," persisting through summer months due to residential wild bird reservoirs—a pattern also seen in the severe summer 2022 seabird mortalities on the Canadian Atlantic coast .

In contrast, risk factors for Peste des petits ruminants (PPR) in the same region focus more on biological and health-status factors, specifically species (goats being at higher risk than sheep) and poor body condition .

Both diseases share common environmental and structural risk factors characteristic of the Ethiopian pastoral system, including seasonal/uncontrolled animal movement, proximity to international borders, and resource scarcity (drought and feed shortages) that forces animals to cluster at communal water and grazing points .
Additionally, brucellosis presents a significant zoonotic risk factor related to the handling of infected reproductive materials, a factor not applicable to the non-zoonotic PPR .

CLINICAL SIGNS IN NEPAL (SKIN NODULES, REDUCED MILK) MATCHED GLOBAL DESCRIPTIONS, THOUGH SYSTEMATIC REVIEWS ADDITIONALLY HIGHLIGHT INTERNAL DAMAGE LIKE TRACHEITIS .

Using a One Health perspective, the risk factors for HPAI H5N1 in Canada are primarily driven by wild bird migration, mammalian spillover into scavengers, and the human-poultry interface .
Surveillance priorities in Canada emphasize genomic monitoring for mammalian adaptation and inter-agency coordination to track wild bird movements .

Surveillance in the Somali region focuses on integrated human-animal sero-surveillance, isolating circulating strains to understand transmission, and addressing sociocultural barriers to disease control and diagnosis [17_brucellosis_ethiopia.pdf:0, 4, 5].

To contrast the data management capabilities of MultiQC and SeqKit with the data collection requirements for zoonotic disease studies in Ethiopia and Cameroon, we must distinguish between digital genomic data processing and field-based epidemiological data collection.
It can parse data for thousands of samples within minutes, enabling researchers to identify global trends, biases, and "abnormal samples" that might indicate batch effects .
The requirements for studying zoonotic diseases like bovine tuberculosis (bTB) in Ethiopia and Cameroon are characterized by intensive field labor and multi-sectoral coordination:

Physical Sampling and Observation: Requirements include the detection of lesions during meat inspections in slaughterhouses and the administration of the Comparative Intradermal Tuberculin Test (CIDT) [14_bovine_tb_cameroon.pdf:0, 9].

While MultiQC and SeqKit provide the efficiency needed to manage the "avalanche of data" from sequencing , they do not address the logistical and interpersonal "data collection tools" (e.g., questionnaires and field supervision) required to navigate the human-wildlife-animal interface in Ethiopia and Cameroon .

Based on the development of Sarek (v3+), nf-core, Snakemake, and fastp, the emerging meta-strategy for balancing efficiency and reproducibility in large-scale genomics is a multi-layered approach centered on modular standardization, aggressive intra-sample parallelization, and infrastructure-agnostic containerization.

DSL2 & Snakefiles: The re-implementation of Sarek in Nextflow DSL2 and Snakemake’s use of "workflow modules" allow for a "one-tool-per-process" design [source_file:03_nfcore_framework.pdf:page 8, 02_snakemake.pdf:page 4].

Centralized Repositories: By using shared repositories like `nf-core/modules` or Snakemake tool wrappers, developers ensure that individual steps (e.g., variant calling with DeepVariant) are standardized across different pipelines, which simplifies maintenance and ensures scientific consistency [source_file:03_nfcore_framework.pdf:page 8, 02_snakemake.pdf:page 4].
To achieve high-performance efficiency, the meta-strategy shifts from parallelizing by sample to parallelizing by data "shards."

Consolidated Pre-processing: `fastp` is a critical tool in this strategy because it combines multiple steps—adapter trimming, quality control, and file sharding—into a single high-performance C++ process [source_file:03_nfcore_framework.pdf:page 0, 3].
This reduces wall-clock time and allows for "population-scale homogeneous recomputing" [source_file:03_nfcore_framework.pdf:page 0, 8].
The strategy relies on immutable software environments to ensure that efficiency gains do not compromise reproducibility.
This ensures that the exact same software version is used regardless of the underlying hardware (local cluster vs. commercial cloud).

Resource-Aware Scheduling: Pipelines now support fine-tuned resource requests (e.g., adjusting CPU/memory for specific intervals) and can utilize spot instances and optimized file systems (like NVME or Fusion) to reduce costs by up to 70% compared to previous iterations [source_file:03_nfcore_framework.pdf:page 10, 11].

This strategy essentially separates scientific logic (the modular tools) from execution logic (the workflow manager) and data-handling efficiency (fastp/sharding), enabling both massive scale and rigorous scientific audit trails.
The collective methodologies of Sarek, Snakemake, nf-core, and MultiQC redefine quality control by shifting it from a single-sample assessment to a multi-layered, system-wide diagnostic process.

Sarek and the nf-core framework integrate QC as a continuous, modular unit within the pipeline, tracking tool versions and execution logs to provide a diagnostic overview of the computational environment alongside biological data [01_sarek:0, 03_nfcore_framework:6].

Snakemake adds a layer of operational diagnostics through "conditional execution," where the workflow's path can be automatically altered (e.g., filtering failed samples) based on intermediate QC metrics [02_snakemake:0].
Together, these tools transform QC into a comprehensive system that monitors data integrity, software performance, and hardware reliability in a single, reproducible framework.

The retrieved documents demonstrate an evolution from localized tool optimization to systemic computational efficiency through three distinct layers of the bioinformatics stack: the tool layer, the workflow orchestration layer, and the infrastructure/ecosystem layer.
The earliest stage of this evolution focuses on localized optimization of specific tasks.

For example, dedicated quality control (QC) tools like FastQC and Qualimap are described as "excellent at highlighting potential problems" but are limited by their localized nature, producing reports on a per-sample basis .
Systemic Shift: MultiQC represents a transition toward efficiency at the analysis layer by aggregating these localized outputs.

Instead of manual compilation (which is "time consuming, repetitive and complex"), MultiQC scans directories to create a single report, allowing for the detection of "global trends and biases" and "batch effects" that are invisible when looking at individual tools or samples .
The stack evolves from running a "complicated collection of software" manually to using sophisticated workflow engines.
Manual execution is identified as "labor-intensive" with high "management overhead" .
Systemic Shift: Workflows like Sarek, built on Nextflow, optimize the process by automatically installing software components and managing the execution of "multiple complex software tools" .

This layer introduces portability, allowing the same pipeline to run across HPC clusters and cloud environments without manual re-configuration, thus shifting efficiency from "task-completion" to "process-reproducibility" .
The most advanced stage of evolution focuses on the entire computational ecosystem, emphasizing cost, speed, and ecological impact.

Storage and I/O Optimization: The corpus highlights a move toward systemic hardware-level efficiencies, such as using NVMe storage and the Fusion file system to accelerate transfer speeds and reduce costs in cloud environments .
Standardization: The nf-core framework itself represents systemic efficiency by providing community-curated, standardized pipelines.

This avoids the "redundancy" of countless in-house workflows and ensures that improvements in one part of the stack (e.g., a more efficient mapping tool) can be propagated across the entire community [source_file:03_nfcore_framework.pdf:2, 11].

** Technical artifact removal (encompassing QC, bias correction, and outlier shrinkage) is the primary determinant of methodological validity in HTS analysis; it prevents technical noise from being misinterpreted as biological variation, thereby minimizing false discovery rates and ensuring the stability of statistical estimates across different experimental conditions.

Human-animal interface factors define the zoonotic risk landscape through the intersection of high-risk professional habits (herding, slaughtering, and raw product consumption), critical livestock physiological events (abortion, aging, and mortality), and environmental stressors* (forage lack and wildlife-livestock contact).
These factors collectively facilitate the maintenance and transmission of bacterial pathogens like M. bovis and Brucella* and viral pathogens like HPAI in endemic regions .

Using bovine tuberculosis (bTB) as a model, the Comparative Intradermal Tuberculin Test (CIDT) often yields lower prevalence than the Simple Intradermal Tuberculin Test (SITT) because it prioritizes specificity .

Furthermore, specific assay thresholds (e.g., 3 mm vs. 4 mm) can lead to a tenfold difference in reported prevalence (6.8% vs 0.6% in Cameroon), demonstrating that international standards may underreport disease in certain local contexts .
These choices impact the identification of risk factors—such as herd size, age, and wildlife contact—and determine the perceived urgency of zoonotic risks and the allocation of veterinary resources .

Anthropogenic factors create patterns of disease persistence by enabling subclinical viral circulation in vaccinated populations, leaving surveillance gaps in pastoralist regions, and maintaining infection through trade-related movement and biosecurity failures.
Specifically, vaccination can lead to "neoteric" subclinical infections where animals shed the virus without showing symptoms, effectively masking the pathogen’s presence [18_fmd_review:2, 5].

The meta-conclusion drawn from the provided research is that traditional early-warning surveillance systems are increasingly inadequate because they rely on overt, uniform clinical signs (passive surveillance) that no longer align with the evolving, highly variable, and often "silent" presentation of modern viral strains.
Traditional surveillance often relies on recognizable indicators like high mortality or distinct lesions (e.g., vesicles in FMD).
Clinical manifestation also varies significantly between virus clades (e.g., H5Nx clade 2.3.4.4b) and the age of the animal (juvenile vs. adult) [source_file:12_hpai_netherlands.pdf:0, 15].

The foot-and-mouth disease virus (FMDV) carrier state is traditionally defined by the isolation of the virus from oropharyngeal fluid (OPF) samples for more than 28 days following infection [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].

While this 28-day threshold is universally accepted for practical purposes, it is based on historical experimental data and holds no specific biological relevance, as many animals clear the infection much earlier [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].

The transitional phase, during which an animal either clears the virus or becomes a carrier, occurs approximately 14–21 days post-infection (dpi) in cattle, though this period is shortened to 7–14 dpi in animals protected by vaccination [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].

The anatomical site of persistence varies by species; in cattle, the virus is consistently detected in the nasopharyngeal mucosa, whereas in sheep and African buffalo, it is primarily localized to the epithelial crypts of the palatine tonsils [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].
In sheep, approximately 80% are carriers at four weeks, but this drops to 25% by 12 weeks [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].
Persistent infection involves a co-adaptation between the host and virus, often characterized by the downregulation of antiviral cytokines [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].
Carriers exhibit a strong local IgA response in oral and nasal secretions, but this fails to clear the virus because the intracellular FMDV remains inaccessible to antibodies [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].

Persistence is further linked to impaired cell-mediated immunity, the impairment of T cell-killing and death receptor pathways, and the potential use of exosomes to shield the virus from the immune system [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].
From a management perspective, FMDV pathogenesis and persistence are central to the regulation of international trade [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].
However, field studies in Vietnam observed a lack of transmission from persistently infected cattle to naïve cattle [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].

Surveillance efforts are informed by the distinction between "neoteric subclinical infection" and the "FMDV carrier state," emphasizing the need to sample clinically unaffected animals [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].
Additionally, diagnostic success is improved by targeting species-specific anatomical sites during sampling, such as the palatine tonsil crypts in sheep and buffalo [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].
High-potency vaccines have been shown to inhibit local virus replication and prevent the carrier state in sheep [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].
Finally, incorporating phases of pre-clinical infectiousness into simulation modeling can significantly improve the prediction of outbreaks in non-endemic regions [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].

The removal of technical artifacts (fastp) and the correction of systematic biases (Salmon) serve as the necessary foundation for reducing false discovery rates.

However, the study notes that this methodology typically underestimates the true prevalence because gross lesion inspection has low sensitivity, missing animals in early stages of infection or those with localized lesions.

This demonstrates how the choice of a 'convenience' diagnostic (slaughterhouse monitoring) can lead to an epidemiological understanding that underestimates the disease burden compared to more sensitive methods like the Tuberculin Skin Test (TST).

The foot-and-mouth disease virus (FMDV) carrier state is traditionally defined by the isolation of the virus from oropharyngeal fluid (OPF) samples for more than 28 days following infection [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].

While this 28-day threshold is universally accepted for practical purposes, it is based on historical experimental data and holds no specific biological relevance, as many animals clear the infection much earlier [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].

The transitional phase, during which an animal either clears the virus or becomes a carrier, occurs approximately 14–21 days post-infection (dpi) in cattle, though this period is shortened to 7–14 dpi in animals protected by vaccination [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].

The anatomical site of persistence varies by species; in cattle, the virus is consistently detected in the nasopharyngeal mucosa, whereas in sheep and African buffalo, it is primarily localized to the epithelial crypts of the palatine tonsils [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].
In sheep, approximately 80% are carriers at four weeks, but this drops to 25% by 12 weeks [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].
Persistent infection involves a co-adaptation between the host and virus, often characterized by the downregulation of antiviral cytokines [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].
Carriers exhibit a strong local IgA response in oral and nasal secretions, but this fails to clear the virus because the intracellular FMDV remains inaccessible to antibodies [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].

Persistence is further linked to impaired cell-mediated immunity, the impairment of T cell-killing and death receptor pathways, and the potential use of exosomes to shield the virus from the immune system [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].
From a management perspective, FMDV pathogenesis and persistence are central to the regulation of international trade [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].
However, field studies in Vietnam observed a lack of transmission from persistently infected cattle to naïve cattle [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].

Surveillance efforts are informed by the distinction between "neoteric subclinical infection" and the "FMDV carrier state," emphasizing the need to sample clinically unaffected animals [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].
Additionally, diagnostic success is improved by targeting species-specific anatomical sites during sampling, such as the palatine tonsil crypts in sheep and buffalo [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].
High-potency vaccines have been shown to inhibit local virus replication and prevent the carrier state in sheep [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].
Finally, incorporating phases of pre-clinical infectiousness into simulation modeling can significantly improve the prediction of outbreaks in non-endemic regions [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].

African swine fever (ASF) has been endemic in Burkina Faso since 2003, with major outbreaks in 2008 and 2018 causing significant losses locally and in neighboring countries such as Benin, Ivory Coast, Niger, Togo, and Ghana [11_asf_burkina_faso.pdf:p0].

The clinical presentation of major viral livestock diseases is shifting away from traditional high-mortality models.

Crucially, in meat-type poultry and ducks, mortality trends can be fluctuating and less dramatic than the exponential increases seen in chickens, making detection through mortality alone less reliable (Wolters et al., 2024; 12_hpai_netherlands.pdf).

Similarly, Lumpy Skin Disease (LSD) presents a high proportion of subclinical cases that facilitate the virus's spread into new territories before the first overt cases are detected (20_lsd_review.pdf).

Traditional early-warning systems, which rely on farmers reporting sudden mortality spikes (passive surveillance), are increasingly inadequate due to these shifting dynamics and the expansion of viruses into wildlife reservoirs.

The meta-conclusion is that surveillance systems must move beyond mortality-only triggers toward multi-parameter criteria including reduced feed/water intake and egg production drops, integrated with active molecular and wildlife monitoring (12_hpai_netherlands.pdf).

Since 2021, H5N1 has spread rapidly across North America via migratory flyways, causing mass mortality in wild bird species such as seabirds, raptors, and gulls [19_hpai_canada.pdf:p0][19_hpai_canada.pdf:p0][12_hpai_netherlands.pdf:p0].

Passive Surveillance Limitations: Detection relies heavily on passive surveillance, which is complicated by the wide variation in clinical signs across different species and age groups [12_hpai_netherlands.pdf:p0][12_hpai_netherlands.pdf:p0].

Inadequate Mortality Criteria: Standard early warning criteria based on mortality ratios are not universally effective; for example, ducks reach specified mortality thresholds less frequently than chickens, potentially delaying detection [12_hpai_netherlands.pdf:p0].

Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) and Lumpy Skin Disease (LSD) both present as subclinical or asymptomatic infections, which complicates traditional passive surveillance systems that rely on the reporting of clinical signs [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0][18_fmd_review.pdf:p0][20_lsd_review.pdf:p0].

In FMD, neoteric subclinical infections occur primarily in animals with acquired immunity or vaccination; these animals shed substantial amounts of virus in oronasal secretions despite showing no clinical symptoms [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0][18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].

This stage is distinct from the "FMDV carrier state," where the virus persists at low levels in the nasopharynx of cattle or the oropharyngeal tonsils of sheep and buffalo for prolonged periods [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0][18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].
Consequently, researchers emphasize that FMD surveillance must include sample collection from clinically unaffected animals to be effective [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].

The provided summaries lead to a high-level meta-conclusion that the evolving clinical presentation of high-consequence viral diseases—characterized by host expansion, subclinical infectiousness, and species-specific symptoms—has rendered traditional, symptom-based passive surveillance systems increasingly inadequate for early detection.

Subclinical Shedding: In diseases like FMD and LSD, animals can be highly infectious while appearing healthy (asymptomatic or neoteric subclinical infections) [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0, 20_lsd_review.pdf:p0].

Pre-clinical Transmission: For FMD, the latent period is often shorter than the incubation period, meaning infectiousness precedes visible lesions, making "waiting for signs" a failed strategy for containment [18_fmd_review.pdf:p0].

Host-Specific Variation: HPAI presents wildly different symptoms depending on the host species (e.g., neurological in ducks and mammals vs. mucosal signs in chickens) and age (juveniles showing more neurological distress), preventing a standardized "early warning" profile [12_hpai_netherlands.pdf:p0, 19_hpai_canada.pdf:p0].
Early-warning systems often use mortality ratios as a trigger for investigation, but these metrics are becoming obsolete:

Inaccurate Thresholds: In HPAI outbreaks, certain species like ducks frequently fail to reach the mortality thresholds used for chickens, leading to delayed detection and continued viral spread [12_hpai_netherlands.pdf:p0].

Infrastructure Gaps: Human healthcare systems often lack the routine subtyping necessary to distinguish HPAI from common seasonal flu, and there is a systemic lack of "One Health" preparedness—specifically in screening patients for animal exposure when they present with unexplained respiratory or neurological symptoms [19_hpai_canada.pdf:p0].
